title: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product-Market Fit

segments.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
segments.text: Rahul, welcome to the podcast. Many founders struggle with knowing whether they actually have product-market fit. You came up with a quantitative framework at Superhuman. How did you define and measure PMF?

segments.speaker: Rahul Vohra
segments.text: When we were building Superhuman in 2017, the prevailing wisdom was Marc Andreessen's definition: you know you have it when the product is flying off the shelves and servers are melting. But that is a lagging indicator. It tells you when you have it, not how to get there. I found Sean Ellis's survey approach: ask your users 'How would you feel if you could no longer use Superhuman?' with three options: very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, and not disappointed.

segments.speaker: Rahul Vohra
segments.text: Sean Ellis benchmarked hundreds of startups and found that the magic threshold is 40%. Companies that struggled to grow almost always had under 40% of users saying they would be 'very disappointed'. Companies with strong traction almost always exceeded 40%. When we first ran this survey on Superhuman in summer 2017, our score was only 22%. We were nowhere near product-market fit.

segments.speaker: Rahul Vohra
segments.text: To systematically increase our score from 22% to 58%, we built the Product-Market Fit Engine. First, segment to find your High-Expectation Customer (HXC). Second, analyze feedback to convert on-the-fence users while doubling down on what the very disappointed group loved. Third, divide your product roadmap 50/50: allocate 50% of engineering bandwidth to doubling down on loved features, and 50% to resolving objections of the somewhat disappointed group.

segments.speaker: Rahul Vohra
segments.text: The key insight about the 'somewhat disappointed' group is you must ignore users who want completely different products. Only pay attention to users whose main objection is a speed bump or missing core integration. If someone wanted Superhuman to be an ERP or project management tool, we politely ignored that feedback to avoid diluting our focus.
